translations.title: The Stone
translations.text:
Through no one's fault will this stone have wept.

It will have slept in the ill omen
of its mother, this stone
plunging through
cerebral union
to the rhythm
of where it came from, aflame
and extinguished. It will have seen
the unseen with
the other eyes of music, and
thus, meekly, lying down
in the frailty of the formless, dry,
opaque, last night without
the sound of an albatross against the closed sky,
it will have gone.

It will not have wavered over this decision
because of the imperfection of its shape, which, being dark, no one ever saw,
for no one ever sees those stones that belong to no one,
in the outgrowth of an opacity
that rather chills them there to the touch like clouds,
neutral, shapeless, without the grace
of marble or the luxury
of turquoise, so ambiguous
if you like, but for that very reason so near!

No, it will not have wavered; it will have emerged
quite intact with its iron-colored
and celestial bearing. At most it will have said to the tree: Farewell,
tree that gave me shade; to the river: Farewell,
river that spoke for me; rain: Farewell,
you who soaked me. Farewell,
white butterfly.

Through no one's fault will this stone have wept.
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.

translations.title: Cunning That Belongs to Her and Cunning That Does Not...
translations.text:
Cunning that belongs to her and cunning that does not,
Ovid would say: heels
belong to her, high ones, if possible; the visible
animal force; the nipples, however
small their form; the kiss
well painted; a Parisian
scent; eyelids blue-tinged
without excess; the stealthy
long-limbed drugged swipe
of her pride; visionary
the gleam, above all that, visionary the gleam.

And of course golden the hundred
and seventy centimeters of her charm,
from ankle to the torrential
strands of hair. “Think,”
Borges suddenly breaks in, breathless, “who
but the Aleph could smell her whole, split and
beastlike so, kiss her on the snout,
endure her, preserve her in her riddle, air her,
mark her to the depths until becoming her, at the full
gallop of tedium? Who,
above all that, could sate her?”

Above all, nothing, boys, seers
of another age! Borges,
Publius Ovid! Nothing: the truth
is there is nothing, except
every twenty-eight days, blood
of childbirth, and that is the game. From there we poets
came, wounded, howling
woman, moaning
beauty, Eternity
that cannot be seen: above all that, boys,
that cannot be seen.
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.

translations.title: The Lovers
translations.text:
Paris, and this is a day in '59, in the air.
It seems the same radiant day has lasted ever since.
Spring knows what it is doing with its kisses. I am still looking for you
in that hurried taxi, among the crowd. It is written that tonight
I will sleep a long time beside your body, and the endless train.

Paris, and this is the match of fierce wonder.
Everything happens in the flash and we have burned without stopping from the start
in our surfeit. Let us love one another through these poor minutes.
The gods stitched us from trains and more trains and wandering planes,
and from ships and ships, this net that binds us on earth.

Paris, and this the sudden swell of eternity.
There we said goodbye so we could keep flying. Do not forget
to write to me. The loss of this skin, these hands,
and those terrible wheels that carry you so far into the night,
and this world opening beneath us so it can go on being born.

Paris, and we go together in the joyful whirl
of this that is born and born with each day's revolution.
To your tall petals I entrust the star of the one who comes in the months of your blood,
and I leave you sleeping on the sheet. I put my hand on the beauty
of your pregnancy, and plainly touch the source.
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.

translations.title: She Who Sleeps There, the Sacred One...
translations.text:
She who sleeps there, the sacred one,
who kisses me and knows me,
the translucent, the vibrant,
the one mad
with love, the high
zither:

you,

no one
but, supple,
you,
the lofty one,
in the high air
of the original
oil
of the Species:

you,

she who spins
at the blind
speed
of the sun:

you,

the elegance
of your natural
presence
so close,
my slope
of diamond, my
harp,
so wondrously mine:

you,

paradise
or
no one,
a string
for hearing
the wind
above the stellar
abyss:

you,

a page
of skin beyond
the air:

you,

hands
I loved,
bare
feet
of the ivory
rhythm
where I placed
my kisses:

you,

volcano
and petals,
flame;
living
tongue
of love:

you,

splendid
figure, orchid
whose airy nature
allows me
to fly:

you,

mortal
girl, fragrance
of another music
of snow,
stealthily
Andean:

you,

daughter of the open,
golden
sea,
you who dance
motionless,
standing
there
in transparency
from
the depths
of the beginning:

you,

mountain range, you,
sleepwalking
chrysalis
in the intangible
radiance
of your corolla:

you,

no one: you:

You,
Poetry,
you,
Spirit,
no one:

you,

who blow
into the wind
these
dark
vowels,
these
measured
chords
in the riddle
of the earthly:

you.
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.

translations.title: Sebastián Acevedo
translations.text:
I see only the man who set himself ablaze in Concepción, who made smoke
of his flesh and burned for all Chile on the steps
of the cathedral before the troops without
blinking, without weeping, lit up and
exploded by a firedamp not of this World: I see
only the man who burned.

I see only Acevedo flaming there
for us, with a man's resolve, stern
and righteous, pine and
adobe, lighting the flight
of the disappeared along the whole
howling coast: I see only the man who burned.

I see only the white flag of his shirt
burn until the four corners of the square
turn red; I see only the lindens
weeping rough nitrogen
for his soul, crying out to heaven
for the return of a toqui
who will lead us out of this: I see only the man who burned.

I see only the deep Bío-Bío, father of waters, keeping watch
over the dead man: healer
of our wounds from Arauco
to today, nearly motionless in
its hoarse sleep and
sacred as the rehue, bearing
the mutilations of the whirl
of sand and blood with bodies at
the bottom, foretelling
resurrection: I see only the man who burned.

I see only the stain of love that
no one can ever tear from the cement, whether they wash it
with turpentine or caustic
soda, scrub it
with steel points, sand it
with nails and bullets, paint over it, deny it
on every screen of
lies from north to south: I see only the man who burned.
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.

translations.title: The Dragon Is a Chimerical Animal, I Am a Dragon...
translations.text:
The dragon is a chimerical animal; I am a dragon
and I love you,
which is to say I love your nose, the surprise
of the sapphire of your eyes;
what I love most is the sapphire of your eyes.

But what plainly turns me thighward is your long
thighs, whose shape sends my sex
and swan flying at once, showing me how perverse
the rose can be, if there is a rose
in touch, silk, scent,

or more than scent and silk, a passage
from one sense to another, given the ungraspable
nature of the painting—I mean
the swiftness of the glorious,
joyous smoothness in you, in the butterfly,

even as years pass, as the famous
ivory piano sounded beneath the smoke in the film; what became
of Humphrey Bogart and that tall Nordic glass
whose slenderness was like a crack? What became
of the white dress?

Decades of skin. Suddenly a man is decades of skin, an urn
of frenzy and
ruin, and the aorta
of living is sadness;
suddenly I myself am sadness.

That is when I speak to your knees and commend myself
to a fleece more lasting
than amaranth, and delve into your poppy with
ritual and abandon;
that is when I delve into your poppy,

and enter the epiphany of immediacy
fanned by freshness, and become touch
with an eye; hurry, and I write phosphorus if
I see at once from nape to foot
mare and alchemy.
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.

translations.title: The Days Go By So Quickly
translations.text:
The days go so quickly in the dark current that all salvation
comes down, for me, to breathing deeply so the air will last in my lungs
one more week; the days go so quickly
toward the invisible ocean that I no longer have blood to swim in safely,
and I am becoming another fish, with my bones.

I return to my origin, I go toward my origin; no one
waits for me there. I run toward the maternal depth
where bone ends; I go to my seed,
for it is written that this must happen among the stars
and in the poor worm that I am, with my weeks
and the happy months I still await.

One is here and does not know one is already gone; it makes you want to laugh
at having entered this delirious game,
but the cruel mirror spells it out one day
and you turn pale and pretend you do not believe it,
pretend you do not hear it, brother, though it is your own sob deep down.

If you are a woman, you put on your most beautiful mask
to deceive yourself; if you are a man, you make
your skeleton harder, but inside it is something else,
and there is nothing, no one, but yourself in this:
so it is best to see the danger clearly.

Let us be ready. Let us stand naked
with what we are, but let us burn, not rot,
what we are. Let us blaze. Let us breathe
without fear. Let us wake to the great reality
of being born now, and in the final hour.
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.

translations.title: The Thing About the Great Larch Is That He Was Born Dead of Thirst...
translations.text:
1. The thing about the great larch is that he was born dead of thirst
and has not quenched it;
not even dying has quenched it, not even going
down the ravine in Valparaíso this Monday, not even then
has he quenched it,
thirsty and magical to the end among the last
larches left to us—“I
am a larch too, and I know what I say!” The thing about this Jorge
Teillier is that he has died.

2. And here I am without anyone, a world-wanderer without him, on the carousel
of Puerta del Sol, empty
among the crowd, wandering
by mistake, walking and weeping
as a man must weep, dry-eyed—the grief
of Arauco beneath it all—a meter
from Madrid's gossip corner, descending
Calle del Arenal in pursuit of Quevedo,
who knew something of the plight
of the loser, and something, something
of the marrow that has burned gloriously.

3. Ah, dust in love, this madman will have
entered the eternity of his alcohol,
which was like his childhood; he will have drunk
lamb's blood again beneath the pouring rain
of Lautaro, which was his kingdom by birth
and apparition; Lihn will have
filled his glass, Yesenin will have
opened the high door to this great man merciless
to himself. Here I leave him
the pact we failed to sign in time; I leave him Isadora's
dance, the kiss,
Mafalda's fresh laughter, though she is gone, the
figure of the instant
from which the World hangs.
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.

translations.title: Coal
translations.text:
I see a swift river shine like a knife, cutting
my Lebu into two fragrant halves. I hear it,
smell it, caress it, travel its length in a child's kiss as I did then,
when wind and rain rocked me. I feel it
like another artery between my temples and my pillow.

It is he. Rain is falling.
It is he. My father comes home drenched. There is a smell
of wet horse. It is Juan Antonio
Rojas on horseback, crossing a river.
Nothing new. The torrential night collapses
like a flooded mine, and lightning shakes it.

Mother, he is almost here: let us open the gate.
Give me that light; I want to greet him
before my brothers. Let me bring him a good glass of wine
to restore him, let him hold me in a kiss
and press the bristles of his beard against me.

Here comes the man, here he comes
covered in mud, enraged by misfortune, furious
at exploitation, starving; here he comes
beneath his Castilian poncho.

Ah, immortal miner, this is your oak house,
the one you built yourself. Come in:
I have come to wait for you; I am the seventh
of your children. It does not matter
that so many stars have crossed the sky in these years,
that we buried your wife one terrible August,
for you and she have multiplied. It does not
matter that the night has been equally dark
for us both.

Come in, do not stand there
looking at me without seeing me, beneath the rain.
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.

translations.title: Portrait of a Woman
translations.text:
Night will always be there, woman, for you to face yourself,
alone before your mirror, free of your husband, naked
with the exact and terrible reality of the great vertigo
that destroys you. You will always have your night and your knife,
and the frivolous telephone to hear my farewell in one slash.

I swore I would not write to you; that is why I call to you through the air
to tell you nothing, as the void says: nothing, nothing,
only the same and always the same of the same
that you never hear from me, that you never understand,
though your veins burn with what I am saying.

Put on the red dress that suits your mouth and your blood,
and burn me in the last cigarette of fear
of great love, and go barefoot through the air by which you came,
the wound of your beauty visible. Pity
the woman who weeps and weeps in the storm.

Do not die on me. I will paint your face in a flash of lightning
just as you are: two eyes to see the visible and invisible,
an archangel's nose and an animal's mouth, and a smile
that forgives me, and something sacred and ageless flying across your brow,
woman, that makes me shudder, for your face is the face of Spirit.

You come and go and adore the sea that sweeps you away in its foam,
and you remain as if motionless, hearing me call from the abyss
of night, and kiss me like a wave.
You were an enigma. You will be an enigma. You will not fly
with me. Here, woman, I leave you your image.
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.

translations.title: As for the Imagination of Stones
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.

translations.title: Farewell to Hölderlin
translations.text:
No one says O rose anymore, nor
even rose except with shame. With shame
at what? At exaggerating
a few petals, the
beauty of a few petals?

Snake is said in every language; that
is what is said, snake
to translate butterfly, because the
fragile one too is banished
from paradise. Computer
is said with ease at parties, computer
in place of thought.

Lyre, what might
a lyre be? Was there
ever anything like
a lyre? A girl
of five strings, perhaps, blond, tall, drunk, weightless,
possessed by beauty, whose
transparency danced?

What song, what singing? Now another
beauty is demanded: less hallucination
and more drugs, far more drugs. What is this business
of stressing the E in Erato or Persephone? Here it is
a question of another, more consistent quartz without
a Faustian farce or
Chorus of Mothers; the chorus
is over, the dithyramb, the famous
ecstasy, the Other, even
with Maldoror, the silky,
voluptuous octopus. There is no
other epiphany than orgasm.

Nor is it possible any longer to name the stars, emptied
as they have been of their radiance, dead,
wandering, without a riddle,
deciphered down to their entrails by
instruments flying from galaxy
to galaxy.

Nor is it so easy to read the
Unknown in smoke; there is no Unknown. They opened
the lid on the marvel of
the brain: there is nothing but a little
stench in the clot of
Genesis lodged there. The seed
of wonder flew away.
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.

translations.title: So They Shot Me in the Left Leg, How Far I Walked!...
translations.text:
So they shot me in the left leg—how far I walked
through the world on this left leg! Not a tree
to say anything to, and vipers, vipers,
 vipers like bullets, and seize him and smash him,
and asthma, and something else,
and asthma, and it is three o'clock. And asthma, asthma, asthma.

So it is three o'clock, or it is no longer three,
nor is it the eighth, nor October. So here ends
the Yuro ravine, so the Ravine
of the World, and it is going to explode. So the big one
is going to explode, and they shot me in October.

So they offered five thousand dollars for this, or was it fifty thousand,
my blood, for what we were and what we are,
and all that we were and are! Five thousand
for my eyes, my hands, fifty thousand for everything,
asthma and all. And that, my hoarse lungs,
when we were going to turn forty singing.

Singing the fateful mosquitoes of death:
rise up, rise up, rise up, you poor; the conduct
of the firing line; welcome the burst
if others come afterward. Come, let us hurry,
hurry to avenge the dead man.

What is mine—what is mine?—this rose, this America
with its old thorns. All dawn long
they judge me in English. What is mine, what is mine,
if not yours, brother? It happened suddenly
and to the heart. Here
the beginning will begin, so swallow your fear.

So they butchered me and then tied me up.
To Vallegrande—why?—and by helicopter!
It is good to water the oxygen with red blood
even if later they burn me and cut off my hands,
both hands.

Keep shooting without stopping
while I go with Bolívar; I will return.
translations.editorial_note: Direct translation; no separate editorial review was conducted.
